identity.title: How Learning Rate Decay Wastes Your Best Data in Curriculum-Based LLM Pretraining

problem.claim: How to better exploit scarce high-quality data in LLM pretraining mixtures using quality-ordered curricula.

gap.claim: Prior curriculum-pretraining studies reported limited improvements; the authors attribute a key constraint to incompatibility between ascending data quality and decaying learning rates.

contributions.claim: Identifies learning-rate decay as a factor that can suppress the benefit of ascending-quality curricula.
Proposes moderate learning-rate decay or weighted averaging of the final checkpoints to mitigate this incompatibility.
Combining the strategies improves average standard-benchmark scores by 1.64% over random shuffling without additional data refinement.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish curriculum performance by the interaction between data-quality ordering and the learning-rate schedule, and introduce simple mitigation strategies based on that interaction.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that curriculum training substantially outperforms random shuffling with a constant learning rate, but its advantage diminishes under standard decay schedules.
The authors report a 1.64% average benchmark-score improvement over random shuffling when combining the proposed strategies, without additional data refinement.
The authors report validation on 1.5B-parameter models trained for 30B tokens with various data-quality metrics.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLM pretraining uses mixed-quality data because high-quality data is scarce.
Quality-ordered curriculum pretraining is a natural strategy, but prior work reported limited gains.
The paper identifies a mismatch between ascending data quality and learning-rate decay as a critical constraint.
Moderate decay and final-checkpoint averaging recover curriculum benefits, with a reported 1.64% combined improvement over random shuffling.
The findings are reported for 1.5B-parameter models, 30B training tokens, and multiple quality metrics, motivating co-design of curricula and optimization.

source_observation.claim: The abstract explicitly links the usefulness of a data curriculum to the learning-rate schedule and reports different curriculum outcomes under constant versus decaying learning rates.

lessons.interpretation: A method's data-ordering component may need to be framed jointly with optimization dynamics rather than evaluated in isolation.
lessons.application: When presenting a curriculum method, state and test the optimizer-schedule assumptions that define when its advantage is expected.
lessons.exception: This framing may be less suitable when data order is fixed, optimization is not schedule-sensitive, or the claim concerns only the data metric.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify benchmark identities, statistical uncertainty, exact schedules, checkpoint weights, or per-metric/per-model results.
It does not quantify the baseline improvement under constant learning rate or establish which mitigation contributes most to the combined gain.
